property_summary: For every call to fallback with any msg.value, the reference contract C only accepts the call (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant that changes the required amount to 5 ether will accept calls with 5 ether and thus violates this acceptance rule for some fuzzed msg.value inputs.

For any caller and any timestamp/block, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) low-level calls to its fallback only when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant accepts when msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs where the reference rejects but the mutant accepts (or vice-versa).

For every caller, the reference contract only accepts (does not revert) low-level calls to its payable fallback when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant that requires 5 ether will accept a different set of msg.value inputs, so there exist fuzzed amounts where the reference rejects but the mutant accepts.

For every caller and amount, the reference contract's payable fallback accepts (does not revert) a call iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant that requires 5 ether will accept different msg.value inputs, so there exist fuzzed amounts where the reference rejects but the mutant accepts.

For every caller and amount, the reference contract only accepts (does not revert) fallback calls when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant changing the required value to 5 ether violates this by accepting calls with 5 ether (so there exist fuzzed amounts where reference rejects but mutant accepts).

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, C always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (monotonic non-decreasing across calls in the correct), while the mutant that removed the timestamp check can be invoked multiple times in the same block causing pastBlockTime to remain equal across repeated calls in that block and thus violate the rule that each successful fallback call sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp when called, which the fuzz can find by calling fallback twice within same block.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C via the payable fallback, each successful fallback invocation sets C.pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant (which removes the timestamp monotonicity check) allows two successful fallback invocations in the same block to leave pastBlockTime equal between calls (violating the rule that each call updates pastBlockTime to the then-current timestamp), so a fuzz that attempts two calls in the same block can distinguish them.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C's payable fallback, each successful fallback invocation updates C.pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant (which removed the require that block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) allows two successful fallback invocations in the same block to both succeed while leaving pastBlockTime equal (i.e., not strictly increasing across invocations), so there exists a sequence of inputs (same block, two calls) where the mutant violates the strict monotonic increase rule.

Every successful call to C's payable fallback that sends exactly 10 ether strictly increases C.pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so two consecutive successful calls in the same block cannot both succeed with the second leaving pastBlockTime unchanged); the mutant that removes the timestamp check allows two calls in the same block leaving pastBlockTime unchanged, violating this strict monotonicity.

For every single successful payable fallback invocation that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so two successful invocations in a row cannot both leave pastBlockTime unchanged), while the mutant (timestamp check removed) allows two successful fallback calls in the same block leaving pastBlockTime equal—violating the strict update rule.

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the stored pastBlockTime equals the block.timestamp after the call; the mutant storing block.number instead of block.timestamp can make pastBlockTime differ from block.timestamp for some inputs.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp increases, the reference contract always records pastBlockTime equal to the current block.timestamp (so address(c).balance is zero when block.number % 15 == 0 due to immediate payout), while the mutant may store block.number instead and thus can leave a nonzero balance when block.number % 15 == 0 (violating the rule).

After any successful payable call to fallback with exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp strictly increases, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime equal to the current block.timestamp (so the getter pastBlockTime == block.timestamp), whereas the mutant sometimes sets pastBlockTime to block.number instead and thus will make pastBlockTime != block.timestamp for some fuzzed inputs.

For any successful payable call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp strictly increases, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so pastBlockTime == block.timestamp), whereas the mutant that assigns pastBlockTime = block.number will cause pastBlockTime != block.timestamp for some fuzzed block timestamps/numbers.

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any caller at a strictly later block.timestamp, the reference contract only pays out when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance becomes 0 iff the current block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant flips the condition and will instead drain the contract on blocks where block.number % 15 != 0, so there exist block numbers where the balances after the call differ.

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any caller at a strictly later timestamp, the reference contract only drains its balance (address(c).balance == 0) when block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant inverts the payout condition and will drain on blocks where block.number % 15 != 0, so there exist fuzzed block numbers that make the post-call balance differ and thus violate the rule.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp, the reference C never drains its entire balance unless the current block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant inverts this condition and will drain on some block numbers where block.number % 15 != 0, so there exist fuzzed block numbers that make address(c).balance differ (zero vs non-zero) after the call.

For any caller, when calling fallback with exactly 10 ether and a strictly increasing timestamp, the reference contract C always increases its stored pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so address(c).balance may grow and pastBlockTime == block.timestamp), but the mutant that refunds msg.value before updating pastBlockTime can leave pastBlockTime unchanged relative to block.timestamp (or leave contract balance unchanged) for some inputs — specifically when the immediate refund prevents the contract from accumulating balance used in the conditional payout path.

For any caller address and block timestamp, when the contract's fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether and block.timestamp advances, the reference always sends any contract balance to the immediate caller (msg.sender) when block.number % 15 == 0, so after such a payout the contract's balance becomes zero — the mutant sending to tx.origin can cause the contract balance to remain non-zero when the immediate caller is a contract (because tx.origin differs from msg.sender), so there exist inputs (a contract caller) that make this property fail.

For any caller and admissible inputs, when fallback is invoked with 10 ether and time advanced, if block.number % 15 == 0 the reference contract always pays out its full balance to msg.sender (leaving address(c).balance == 0), but the mutant paying tx.origin can leave address(c).balance != 0 when the immediate caller is a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin).

For any caller that is a contract and any block where block.number % 15 == 0, when sending exactly 10 ether through fallback after time advances the reference C always empties its balance (pays the immediate caller msg.sender) whereas the mutant paying tx.origin can leave C with a nonzero balance when msg.sender != tx.origin.

For every call where block.timestamp increases and exactly 10 ether is sent, if block.number % 15 == 0 then the reference contract always transfers its entire balance to the immediate caller (msg.sender) leaving address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that uses tx.origin can leave address(c).balance != 0 when the immediate caller is a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin).

For any caller contract and any admissible inputs where fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether and block.timestamp advances, if block.number % 15 == 0 then the reference contract always forwards its entire balance to msg.sender (so address(c).balance == 0), while the mutant sending to tx.origin can leave address(c).balance > 0 when the immediate caller is a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin).
